solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Family maybe present tons in journal (10)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the tons inside the journal, so T is set within DIARY

blocks.note: present = in attendance, at this place
a daily record kept by hand; T goes between DI and ARY

annotation.surface: Someone presents a family's worth of tons of material in a journal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a verb or a gift; it is the adverb for being here. 'Family' works as an adjective, as in a family trait, and 'maybe' marks it as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a family trait, like a family nose, is one passed down the bloodline, which is what hereditary describes.

blocks.note: a verb: to spray clean with a garden pipe
drawers here means legwear, and 'old' points to the breeches and stockings of earlier centuries

annotation.surface: An instruction to launder some antique underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' reads as furniture or knickers; here it is old legwear, and HOSE is the period word for it, as in doublet and hose.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: hosing a car down washes it, and hose were the breeches or stockings men wore in Tudor times.

blocks.note: a line of mountains, or a product line

annotation.surface: A business maxim: what the bottom line shows forces change.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottom line' reads as the accountant's phrase, and has to be split into two separate words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to change the layout of a room is to shuffle its furniture into a new order.

blocks.note: the surface pushes a figure from Greek drama; the setter means a letter of the Greek alphabet
not the play's heroine but the middle of the word M-E-D-E-A, which is D

annotation.surface: A question about the main figure in Euripides' tragedy Medea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in the play, and Medea is its central character; but the character central to the word MEDEA is D, and the Greek D is DELTA.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as a riddle: the letter at the centre of M-E-D-E-A is D, whose Greek name is delta.

indicatorNotes.over: turning something over flips it end to end, so the string is read backwards

blocks.note: a spin is a turn, a rotation
a groove worn or cut in the ground

annotation.surface: A farming tip: plough the furrow over to grow vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn' looks like the TURN at the front of the answer, but that TURN comes from RUT read backwards; 'Turn' itself is SPIN.
annotation.definitionFit: A plural noun matched by a plural: turnips are the white root vegetables grown in furrowed fields.

entries.clue: Baloney’s put round hole getting mice? (7)

indicatorNotes.put round: to put something round another is to wrap it about it, so ROTS encloses the hole

annotation.surface: Someone talking nonsense has stuffed a hole and ended up with mice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Baloney' sounds like the sausage, but it means nonsense (ROT). The question mark admits mice are only one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: mice are one kind of rodent, and the question mark signals the part standing for the whole.

entries.clue: Long extended poem is classical, initially (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: 'initially' means at the start, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the first letters of Extended Poem Is Classical

annotation.surface: A description of an epic: a long poem in the classical tradition.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes an epic poem, but only 'Long' is the definition, used as an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: an epic queue or an epic journey is a very long one.

entries.clue: Perhaps bowl over fielding hard shot (5)

indicatorNotes.fielding: a fielder stops and holds the ball, so POT O takes hold of the H

blocks.note: a bowl is one kind of pot, hence 'Perhaps'

annotation.surface: Cricket: a bowler's over, fielders and a hard-hit shot.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything sounds like cricket, but 'bowl' is a container, 'over' is just O, and 'shot' means a snapshot, not a stroke.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from photography: a shot is a single picture taken with a camera.

entries.clue: Devoted time, ultimately cracking criminal’s case (10)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: 'ultimately' means in the end, so only the final letter is used
indicatorNotes.cracking: cracking something means breaking into it, so E breaks in between CONS and CRATE

annotation.surface: A dedicated detective finally cracks a criminal case.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a detective story; the answer is an old adjective meaning consecrated.
annotation.definitionNote: CONSECRATE here is the archaic adjective, equal to consecrated
annotation.definitionFit: An old adjectival use: something consecrate has been devoted or dedicated to a sacred purpose.

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom, so the letters are reversed

blocks.note: an air is a bearing or manner

annotation.surface: A partner has gone, and the one left behind is holding up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bearing up' reads as coping bravely; 'bearing' is a noun for manner, and 'up' is the down-clue reversal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the material world is the physical one, as opposed to the spiritual.

indicatorNotes.last: 'last' names the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a staple is a standard, basic item, as in a staple diet

annotation.surface: The last days of a standard office photocopier.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copier' sets the scene in an office, which is where the answer lives too.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the stapler is a fixture of every office desk.

indicatorNotes.capturing: to capture is to take prisoner and hold, so DRAG ON holds the O inside it

blocks.note: to drag on = to continue tediously; split as DRAG + ON

annotation.surface: A slow advance that captures an old soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a war story, and 'old soldier' reads as one phrase; 'old' is split off to be captured.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical term: dragoons were soldiers who rode to battle and fought on foot.

entries.clue: Conservative helping to preserve English life (8)

indicatorNotes.to preserve: to preserve something is to keep it safely inside, so RATION holds the E

blocks.note: a ration is a helping or portion

annotation.surface: Conservative efforts to preserve the English way of life.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is political; 'life' is the definition in the sense of all living things.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: all creation means every living thing, the whole of life on earth.

indicatorNotes.heart: the heart of a word is its centre, here the middle letter of sweet

blocks.note: to lope is to run with long easy strides

annotation.surface: Running off with a lover.
annotation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines the answer; read in parts, 'sweetheart' is the heart of sweet and 'Run' is LOPE, with 'with' joining them.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: to elope is to run away secretly with a lover to marry.

entries.clue: Drink, taking one’s time, being anxious (10)

indicatorNotes.taking: to take something is to take it in, so DRAUGHT absorbs the letters

blocks.note: a draught is a swallow of drink

annotation.surface: Someone sips a drink slowly because they are nervous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking one's time' reads as an idiom for going slowly; it has to be broken up.
annotation.definitionNote: DISTRAUGHT is an adjective; 'being anxious' is a descriptive phrase for the same state
annotation.definitionFit: A strengthened synonym: distraught is a state of acute anxiety or distress.

entries.clue: Batting turn proceeds, possibly losing wicket (7)

indicatorNotes.losing: to lose something is to be left without it, so the W goes

blocks.note: winnings are one kind of proceeds, hence 'possibly'
w = wicket, a cricket scoring abbreviation; removed

annotation.surface: A cricket side's batting turn goes on, perhaps after a wicket falls.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Proceeds' reads as a verb for the game going on; it is a noun, the money taken. An innings is a side's turn to bat in cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: A cricket term: an innings is the spell in which one side or player bats.

entries.clue: Just dropping ecstasy, almost snorting line (8)

indicatorNotes.dropping: to drop something is to let it go, so E falls out of NEARLY
indicatorNotes.snorting: to snort a drug is to take it in through the nose, so NARLY takes in ROW

blocks.note: E = ecstasy, the drug; removed, leaving NARLY
a row is a line of things

annotation.surface: Someone who only just quit ecstasy is nearly doing a line of cocaine.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about drugs; 'Just' is the definition, as in only just.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of 'only just': to win narrowly is to win by a whisker.

blocks.note: s = small, as on clothing labels
a smoked, split herring, a British breakfast dish

annotation.surface: A ship's captain has caught a small fish.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's after 'Captain' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. A kipper is a smoked herring.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: the skipper is the captain of a boat or a sports team.

blocks.note: prose is ordinary language, not verse

annotation.surface: A lawyer's plain speech about an appeal against a charge.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom, where the answer belongs too; 'appealing' means attractive, not lodging an appeal.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal synonym in the verb sense: to charge someone with a crime is to prosecute them.

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in the sense of around: the words sit around the answer

annotation.surface: Someone is cheerful or cold about a proposal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blithe' and 'emotionless' look like two moods to choose between; together they hold the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A mathematical sense: a theorem is a proposition proved from axioms.

indicatorNotes.During: 'during' means within a span, so the answer lies within the words

blocks.note: surface padding: only the 'time' of half-time is used

annotation.surface: At half-time in a match, the team collected a cup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-time' looks like an instruction to halve TIME; it is only surface, and the answer runs through 'time, men took'.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a trophy can be any keepsake of an event, such as a stag's head from a hunt.

indicatorNotes.aired: to air something is to broadcast or voice it, so the words are said out loud

annotation.surface: A dissenter voiced a complete question about everything.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aired' can pass for voicing an opinion, which fits a dissenter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a holdout refuses to go along with the majority.

entries.clue: Crop top with stiff cut top (7)

indicatorNotes.cut: to cut something short is to trim its end, so HARD loses its D
indicatorNotes.top: in a down clue, 'top' means placed above, so HAR goes first

blocks.note: deletion indicator: the last letter D goes
a vest is a top, a sleeveless garment

annotation.surface: A fashion item: a crop top paired with a stiff, cut-down one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crop top' reads as the short garment, but 'Crop' is the definition and the first 'top' is VEST; the final 'top' puts HAR above it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: the harvest is the crop that has been gathered in.

entries.clue: Warning missing Republican essentially about battle (5)

indicatorNotes.missing: to be missing something is to lack it, so R is removed
indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is its core, its middle letter

annotation.surface: A warning about a battle, lacking a Republican's voice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a link to the battle, but it supplies its middle letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper name: the Alamo was the 1836 siege in the Texas revolution, remembered in 'Remember the Alamo'.

indicatorNotes.Occasionally: 'occasionally' means now and then, so only every other letter appears

blocks.note: the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in Cambridge, Massachusetts

annotation.surface: A Cambridge college now and then wins a land grant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cambridge university' suggests the English one; it is the American MIT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to grant a point in argument is to admit it.

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts one thing inside another, so OR sits inside MASSES

annotation.surface: Piles of gold heaped up in a mess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumbles' looks like a verb; it is the plural noun, matching MORASSES.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a morass is a boggy mess, and hence any confused jumble.

indicatorNotes.including: to include something is to take it in, so SPAN holds the I
indicatorNotes.principal: the principal letter is the chief, leading one: the first

blocks.note: a span is a stretch of distance or time

annotation.surface: A stretch of land taking in Iberia's main country.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is itself Iberia's principal country, so the surface reads straight.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Spain is the largest country on the Iberian peninsula.

indicatorNotes.surrounded by: something surrounded is enclosed on all sides, so PET wraps around R

blocks.note: a treasure is a darling, a pet

annotation.surface: A bold queen sits among her treasure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Treasure' reads as riches, but it means a darling, as in 'you're a treasure'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pert reply is a bold, cheeky one.

indicatorNotes.periodically: 'periodically' means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

annotation.surface: An orchestra's members play and learn from time to time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a musical verb in this setting; it is the noun GAME.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind: a gamelan is an Indonesian orchestra of gongs, drums and metallophones.

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following in order, so SURE comes behind ERA

blocks.note: an era is a period of time

annotation.surface: A grim truth: in time, being wiped out is certain.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a sombre proverb; 'is' is only a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: erasure is the act of rubbing something out until no trace is left.

indicatorNotes.opening: the opening of a word is where it begins, its first letter

annotation.surface: A critic sneers at an exhibition opening in a gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: The TATE is a group of British art galleries, the best known in London; the surface is a sneer at modern art.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper name: the Tate is Britain's national gallery of British and modern art.

entries.clue: Party with government’s leader in Asia? (10)

indicatorNotes.leader: the leader goes at the front, so the first letter is taken
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts one thing inside another, so G sits inside the continent

blocks.note: Asia is one example of a continent, hence the question mark

annotation.surface: A political party joins an Asian government's leader.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests politics, but it means a group, as in a party of soldiers.
annotation.definitionFit: A group sense: a contingent is a party sent as part of a larger body, like a contingent of troops.
